newsitem.title: USA: Applied Materials sees downturn into 1997.
newsitem.headline: Applied Materials sees downturn into 1997.

text.p: Applied Materials Inc, the world's biggest supplier of equipment used in making semiconductors, said on Thursday it expected an industrywide downturn to extend through the first half of 1997.

The company said its orders in the quarter ended October 27 fell 43 percent to $683.2 million from $1.2 billion in the 1995 fiscal fourth quarter -- a time when the industry was booming. The 1996 third quarter brought $931.3 million in orders.
On a positive note, Applied announced a $117 million order from Hyundai Corp's American unit.
Applied's total backlog at the end of fiscal 1996 was $1.4 billion, down from $1.5 billion at the end of fiscal 1995.

"Looking forward, we believe the industry downturn could extend through the early part of 1997, with the last half of 1997 still uncertain. We are cautiously optimistic that memory device prices and inventory levels are stabilizing in our customers' business," said James Morgan, chairman and chief executive officer, in a statement.
The company's fourth-quarter earnings fell 53 percent to $0.40 per share, and revenues fell 12.4 percent to $861.0 million from the quarter a year ago.

Wall Street analysts had forecast a mean of $0.48 a share, excluding special charges, according to First Call. With a provision of $0.09 a share for restructuring, Applied's results were close to the average estimate.
"I'd take these results as pretty much in line with expectations," said PaineWebber analyst Gunnar Miller.

Early in the fourth quarter, Applied Materials management warned that earnings and revenues would fall short of year-ago levels and offered some guidance as to a likely range. The company also said the downturn could last into 1997.
Semiconductor equipment makers, which entered a slowdown after the chip industry itself, is now expected to lag in the recovery.

Sales and orders at many semiconductor companies have rebounded from their nadir of mid 1996. However, excess inventory was a big reason for the slump, so most chip makers have been slow to expand capacity with new plants or equipment.
